paper_metadata.title: Age, symptoms, and functional outcome after mild traumatic brain injury

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used a consecutive recruitment strategy from a single emergency department, providing a clear sampling frame. Inclusion/exclusion criteria and baseline characteristics are well-defined, though the 'mild spectrum' definition is broad.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: adult patients between the ages 18 and 100 (n = 325) evaluated for head injury upon presentation to the Tampere University Hospital Emergency Department (ED)
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as adult patients presenting to a specific ED for head injury.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: The sample represents a cohort of sequentially recruited patients who presented to a single ED in Finland following a mild head injury.
items.reasoning: Sequential recruitment from a primary point of care (ED) minimizes selection bias compared to referral-based recruitment.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between November 2015 and November 2016.
items.reasoning: The exact dates of the recruitment window are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Tampere University Hospital Emergency Department (ED) between November 2015 and November 2016.
items.reasoning: The specific hospital and department are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Exclusion criteria included GCS < 13 (n = 5), undergoing neurosurgery or another type of surgery due to the acute injury (n = 7), having a second head injury within a week of the first injury (n = 2), or dying within a week of the injury (n = 2).
items.reasoning: Specific clinical and temporal exclusion criteria are listed.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: All participants provided written informed consent according to the Declaration of Helsinki.
items.reasoning: The study implies a high participation rate among those eligible in the ED during the period, though the exact number of refusals is not explicitly stated.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2: Age group differences on demographic, pre-injury health and functioning, and injury characteristics
items.reasoning: Table 2 provides a comprehensive breakdown of age, sex, pre-injury MRS, dementia, and injury severity markers.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: There is a high risk of attrition bias. 27% of the sample was excluded due to missing outcome data, and this missingness was significantly associated with older age and pre-existing cognitive/functional impairment, which are key variables in the prognostic model.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Among this sample, 88 participants had missing data on the Rivermead Post Concussion Symptoms Questionnaire (RPQ) at 1 week post injury... These individuals were also excluded
items.reasoning: 88 out of 309 (28.5%) were excluded due to missing data, which is a high rate for a 1-week follow-up.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The authors do not describe specific efforts made to reach those who did not provide RPQ data.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: The substantial missingness of RPQ data is likely attributable to pre-existing conditions resulting in functional or cognitive impairments that could impact the capacity of patients to actively participate
items.reasoning: The authors hypothesize reasons (cognitive impairment) but do not provide confirmed reasons for each dropout.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1: Differences in demographic, pre-injury health and functioning, and injury characteristics related to missingness on the RPQ
items.reasoning: The study provides a detailed comparison of those with and without missing data.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Individuals with missing RPQ were older and more likely men. They were much more likely to have pre-existing functional impairment, dementia, and neurological conditions.
items.reasoning: Significant differences exist between completers and non-completers, suggesting informative censoring.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (Age) is objective and reliably measured. Secondary factors (pre-injury status) were collected from electronic records and retrospective report, which is standard.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: participants were grouped as <65 years old and ≥65 years old.
items.reasoning: Age is clearly defined and dichotomized based on established geriatric thresholds.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The medical history of each participant was available through their electronic record
items.reasoning: Age and medical history were verified via electronic health records, which are highly reliable.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Consistent with previous research on age-related differences in TBI,18,19 participants were grouped as <65 years old and ≥65 years old.
items.reasoning: The cut-point of 65 is standard in clinical literature and not derived from the study's own data distribution.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The medical history of each participant was available through their electronic record, which included a local hospital and all healthcare centers in Tampere, Finland.
items.reasoning: A centralized electronic record system was used for all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.reasoning: Age data was available for the entire initial sample.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation was used; cases with missing outcome data were simply excluded.

quips_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the tools (RPQ, MRS) are validated, the lack of blinding (assessors knew CT results) and the use of phone interviews (which can yield different results than self-administration) introduce potential measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: evaluated at 1 week post injury on the Modified Rankin Scale and Rivermead Post Concussion Symptoms Questionnaire (RPQ).
items.reasoning: Outcomes and the specific follow-up interval (1 week) are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Both the nurse and participant were not blinded to CT findings prior to the administration of both measures.
items.reasoning: The tools are valid, but the lack of blinding of the assessor (nurse) to injury severity (CT) increases the risk of bias.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A nurse with neurological training administered the Finnish-language versions of the Modified Rankin Scale (MRS) and RPQ by phone at approximately 1 week post injury.
items.reasoning: All participants were assessed via the same phone-based protocol.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study measures many important confounders (pre-injury disability, dementia, injury signs). However, the analysis relies on correlations and univariate comparisons rather than multivariable modeling to adjust for these factors simultaneously.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: pre-existing conditions included Dementia... mental and behavioral disorders... and diseases of the nervous system
items.reasoning: Key geriatric confounders were captured.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: coded as present or absent based on the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition (ICD-10).
items.reasoning: ICD-10 codes provide standardized definitions for confounders.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Medical history information and injuryrelated data were collected retrospectively from available records
items.reasoning: Use of medical records is generally more reliable than patient recall for pre-existing conditions.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Each record was reviewed for pre-existing conditions... available through their electronic record
items.reasoning: The same record review process was applied to all.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation was mentioned.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: participants were grouped as <65 years old and ≥65 years old.
items.reasoning: Stratification by age was used, but other confounders were not balanced by design.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Spearman ρ correlations were calculated... Using a Mann-Whitney U test
items.reasoning: The study used univariate tests and correlations rather than multivariable regression to adjust for confounders like pre-injury MRS or dementia.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis is straightforward but limited. The lack of multivariable adjustment and the exclusion of a large portion of the sample (attrition) without sensitivity analysis or imputation limits the validity of the conclusions.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Significance was set at P < .05... Spearman ρ correlations were calculated... Mann-Whitney U test
items.reasoning: The statistical methods are clearly stated.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Due to the exploratory nature of the study, there was no a priori correction made for multiple comparisons.
items.reasoning: The study is exploratory and lacks a formal multivariable model building strategy.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Spearman ρ correlations were calculated between ∆MRS and the RPQ total score
items.reasoning: Non-parametric tests are appropriate for the data distribution, but do not allow for adjustment of confounders.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 3: Differences in symptom endorsement frequencies by age group
items.reasoning: The study reports on all 16 RPQ symptoms and multiple composite scores, regardless of significance.
